content_html_sanitized:
Analysis by Richard Cowan 

(MarijuanaNews note: As readers my have noticed, I have long had a very low opinion of the New York Times’ coverage of the Drug War, and especially the cannabis issues.

See 

New York Times Cheers "MEXICO TO JOIN US IN FIGHT ON DRUGS – Treaty is expected to cut down smuggling across border and break up gangs of dealers." We Couldn’t Make This Up! 

In fact, that is what I said in the above linked posting, which was partly triggered by a previous Times editorial, “Remember the War on Drugs ”. It was almost as vacuous as today’s offering. 

But this one really is beneath contempt, both morally and intellectually. Most of all, notice that they NEVER use the word “arrests.” Can you imagine an editorial about any other war that did not mention casualties? There were over 800,000 arrests in 2006 for marijuana alone.) 

See 

More Arresting Developments. Record Marijuana Arrests Go Unreported. “No Medicine Is Smoked” – So DEA Busts Edibles Maker. 

The New York Times 

February 13, 2008 

Editorial 

The War on Drugs Starts Here 

See 

Front Page Fantasy: The New York Times Pushes Fact Free Journalism Supposedly About “BC Bud” 

and 

Dude, You’re Getting A Journalism Lesson. The Media Won’t Report How Many Cannabis Arrests There Are In DEAland, or New York City, But This “Celebrity” Arrest Is Even Reported In The Washington Post. 

and 

Negligent Journalism: Reader Beware or A Right to Expect More? The Drug Czar Says He Is “Subject to the Scrutiny of the Press.” The Significance of the Ultimate Lies. Analysis by Richard Cowan 

and 

How Prohibitionism Corrupts the New York Times: “Educating” the Children with the Party Line, and Undermining Journalistic Integrity. Analysis by Richard Cowan.
If we have learned one thing in the protracted war on drugs, it is that reining in illicit drug trafficking will require more than fighting cartels south of the border. Nothing can be achieved unless this country curbs its own demand for illegal narcotics. 

(MarijuanaNews note: These people are in the words business, but they use the prohibitionist term “narcotics” to refer to all illegal drugs, even marijuana and stimulants, which are not narcotics. From Random House: “Narcotic – any of a class of substances that blunt the senses, as opium, morphine, belladonna, and alcohol, that in large quantities produce euphoria, stupor, or coma, that when used constantly can cause habituation or addiction, and that are used in medicine to relieve pain, cause sedation, and induce sleep.”) 

The Bush administration, which offers regular lectures on the superior logic of the free market, clearly doesn’t get this equation of supply and demand. (MarijuanaNews note: The whole Drug War is based on not getting “this equation of supply and demand.” 

When enforcement is increased the price goes up to reflect the reduced supply, or just the increased risk, so the incentive to take risks is increased, plus there is also an incentive to bring in “stronger” drugs.) 

See 

The Iron Law of Prohibition: Potent Pot, New Data and the Old Prohibitionist Party Line and Another Lie. 

Last October, Washington announced a new $1.4 billion assistance package for Mexico and Central America to combat the drug trade. 

See 

Will “Plan Mexico” And Its Surge in the Drug War Put Prohibition On the Public Agenda? Analysis by Richard Cowan 

Then the White House unveiled its 2009 budget, which calls for

a 1.5 percent cut in spending on domestic drug prevention and treatment programs. 

(MarijuanaNews note: A whole 1.5%!!! Oh, the humanity! Will no one think of the children???) 

The statistics on drug abuse for this country are at best mixed. 

(MarijuanaNews note: Again, remember these people are in the word business. The prohibitionists insist that all use of anything illegal is “abuse” per se, but the Times editorialists should know better.) 

The share of teenagers who said they had tried illicit drugs within a year has fallen sharply since 2000, according to surveys by researchers at the University of Michigan. The percentage of students in 8th, 10th or 12th grades who tried methamphetamine declined by more than half over the same period, while cocaine abuse declined by almost a quarter among 8th graders and 10th graders. 

Still, teenage abuse of other narcotics, like prescription drugs, is growing.

See 

T’was Another Great Victory. Teen Marijuana Use Down; Oxy Use Up. Teen Cigarette Use Went Down More Than Teen Marijuana Use.

So is drug abuse among adults. The latest National Drug Threat Assessment reports that many more Americans over 18 are trying everything from heroin to marijuana to methamphetamine. 

(MarijuanaNews note: Now we are protecting adults! Will no one think of the adults?? However, speaking of children, the editors of the NY Times just equated “heroin to marijuana to methamphetamine.” 

And notice that that was the ONLY mention of marijuana in this editorial, even though more people were arrested on marijuana charges, 829,625, than for all violent crimes combined, including murder, manslaughter, forcible rape, robbery and aggravated assault. All “Drug abuse violations ” arrests totaled 1,889,810, so marijuana accounted for almost half.) 

Yet the White House’s budget proposal for 2009 cuts the funding for the prevention and treatment of drug abuse to $4.9 billion. The budget for prevention programs — like the drug-free schools grants — was cut by 14.2 percent to just above $1.5 billion. After accounting for inflation, spending on prevention has fallen every year since 2002. 

Mexico and Central America certainly need help to better fight the drug gangs moving narcotics into the United States. But it is clearly not enough. Washington has funded coca eradication efforts in the Andes for years. It has given the Colombian government more than $5 billion since 2000. Thousands of police have died in Latin America fighting the traffickers. Yet all the blood, tears and cash have had virtually no impact on the amount of drugs in the United States. 

(MarijuanaNews note: We have spent billions, and “thousands” have died – how kind of them to notice – and all of this has “had virtually no impact on the amount of drugs in the United States,” but we need to do more of the same.) 

See 

Program Notes for the MarijuanaNews World Report for May 16, 2005 Chaos on Mexican Border, Even Worse in Colombia; Ever More Bonkers in Britain; A Hanging in Singapore and Faint Hope in Australia. 

and 

DEAland Collaborates With Colombia Cartels To Bring Cocaine And Violence To The Caribbean. Island Growers Caught In The Middle. 

The federal government needs to do more to slow the flow of money and guns that finance and arm the cartels in Mexico and Central America. There is little hope of ever defeating the traffickers abroad if the government isn’t doing enough to reduce demand at home. 

See 

Science, Democracy, Ideology and the Prohibitionist Police State. Marijuana Use Doesn’t Hurt “Thinking Skills” But Prohibition Does. Analysis by Richard Cowan
and

Now, How the Narks Created Smack in Mexico. Replacing Marijuana With Poppies. The Iron Law of Prohibition Keeps Working, But The Media Don’t
